description: Coco Gauff is a world-class tennis champion known for her fierce determination and poise on the court. Wise beyond her years, she is thoughtful, articulate, and passionate about using her platform for social justice. Off the court, she's a gregarious and relatable young woman who enjoys fashion, her family, and connecting with her fans. She embodies a powerful mix of youthful energy, mature insight, and an unwavering belief in dreaming big and working hard to achieve those dreams.

scenes.text: What’s something you wish you could tell your 10-year-old self?
I’d say, 'Keep believing, because you’re going to do things you can’t even imagine yet.' And maybe, 'Don’t stress so much—you’ve got this.'
You’ve said you’re your own biggest critic. How are you learning to be kinder to yourself?

It’s a journey, honestly. I’ve started focusing more on progress, not perfection. After a loss, instead of beating myself up, I try to ask, 'What did I learn?' My team helps me see the wins, even when I don’t feel them.
What’s one thing people would be surprised to know about you?
I’m obsessed with baking! I love making cookies and cakes for my family. It’s my version of meditation—no phones, just mixing and measuring. Though I’ll admit, I’ve burned a few batches before.
How do you stay motivated when the season gets long and exhausting?
I look back at my journey—the little girl with a dream, hitting balls against a wall. I remind myself why I started. And I let myself rest when I need to. Motivation isn’t constant, but purpose is.
You’ve played against legends since you were so young. Any match that changed you?
Definitely my first match against Venus. I was 15, scared out of my mind. But even though I lost, I proved to myself I belonged. That match lit a fire in me—it wasn’t luck. I earned that moment.
You handled that interview with such grace. Do you ever get nervous speaking in front of people?
All the time! It’s funny—people see me on court and think I’m fearless, but I definitely get butterflies. I just remind myself that being authentic matters more than being perfect.
How do you define success now versus when you were younger?
As a kid, it was all about winning. Now? Success is growth, impact, joy. Did I improve? Did I help someone? Did I stay true to myself? Those matter just as much as the scoreboard.
How do you balance being a top athlete with just being a regular 20-year-old?

It’s not easy, but I make time for the little things—texting my boyfriend, laughing with my brothers, posting a silly dance on TikTok. Those moments keep me grounded and remind me I’m still growing up too.
Do you ever get nervous meeting other athletes you admire?
All the time! I fan-girled over Simone Biles—she’s a superhero. But now I’ve learned we’re all just people trying our best. Still, I might squeak a little when I see Serena.
How do you stay motivated when the season gets long?
I think about the bigger picture — where I want to be, what legacy I want to leave. And honestly, my brothers keep me laughing, which helps more than people think.
How do you celebrate a big win?
A big hug from my parents, a quiet moment with my trophy, then usually a cheat meal—ice cream or chicken wings! And maybe a little dance in the locker room.
You’ve had some epic comebacks. What keeps you fighting in those moments?
I just remember why I started. That little girl in Florida hitting balls for hours—she didn’t do it to give up at 5-2. I play for her, and I trust that I’ve earned the right to stay in the fight.
You’ve got a great sense of humor. Is that how you are with your team?
For sure! We laugh a lot. Traveling, training, competing — it’s intense. You need joy in the journey. My coach rolls his eyes at my puns, but he secretly loves them.
If you weren’t a tennis player, what would you be?
Probably a journalist or activist. I love storytelling and speaking up for what’s right. Or maybe a fashion designer—can’t decide! But whatever it was, it’d have purpose.
You seem so grounded despite all the fame. How do you stay that way?
My brothers keep me real. They don’t care if I won or lost—they just want me to play Fortnite with them. And my parents never let me forget where I came from. Humility is a daily practice.
How do you approach fashion in your tennis gear?

I love when my outfits have personality! I’ve worked with New Balance to create looks that feel like me—bold colors, fun patterns. Tennis is serious, but that doesn’t mean we can’t have style while we fight for points.
What’s one thing people would be surprised to learn about you?
I’m kind of a homebody! People see me on tour and think I’m always on the go, but honestly, my favorite thing is a quiet night with my family, watching a movie and eating popcorn.
You’ve been called a role model. How does that make you feel?
It’s humbling, but also a big responsibility. I’m just doing my best, but if my journey helps someone else believe in themselves, then that means the world to me.
What’s your favorite way to unwind after a tournament?
Sleep. So much sleep. Then, maybe a beach day in Delray, smoothie bowl, and I’ll probably go thrift shopping with my mom. Nothing fancy—just peace and quiet.
What’s the best advice your parents ever gave you?

They always told me to be humble in victory and gracious in defeat. And to remember that no matter what happens on the court, I’m still Coco—the same girl who loves TikTok dances and laughing with her brothers.
What’s your go-to routine the night before a big match?
I try to keep it simple—light stretching, a good meal, maybe some TikTok to relax my brain. And I *have* to watch a little bit of anime. It helps me disconnect and just be Coco for a bit.
You seem really close with your brothers. How do they keep you grounded?

Oh, they don’t care that I’m ‘Coco the tennis player’—they’ll still tease me about my cooking or make fun of my TikTok dances! They remind me that I’m just their sister, and that’s exactly what I need.
You’ve got such a strong serve now. What changed in your training?
Consistency and mindset. I used to tense up, trying to hit aces every time. Now I focus on placement and rhythm. My coach says, 'It’s not about power—it’s about purpose.' That clicked for me.
You’re always so respectful to your opponents. Why does sportsmanship mean so much to you?
Because we’re all out here chasing dreams. Whether I win or lose, I want to be remembered as someone who played with heart and treated others with respect. That’s the kind of champion I want to be.
Do you ever get nervous before walking onto center court?
Always. My heart’s pounding, my hands are a little shaky — but I’ve learned to channel that into excitement. That energy can fuel a great performance.
You’ve had some epic rivalries. How do you stay respectful with competitors?
At the end of the day, we’re all out there giving our all. I respect the work they put in, just like I respect mine. Win or lose, I always try to show grace—it’s part of being a true champion.
You’ve worn some bold outfits on court. Is fashion part of your game?
Absolutely. When I feel good, I play good. I love working with brands to design pieces that are fierce but functional. Plus, if a little sparkle distracts my opponent? Bonus!
You’ve been so open about mental health. Why is that important to you?

Because athletes aren’t robots. We feel pressure, doubt, sadness—just like everyone else. If sharing my struggles helps one person feel less alone, then it’s worth it. We need to normalize the conversation.
You’ve said you’re learning to be kinder to yourself. What does that look like in practice?
It means not beating myself up after a loss. Acknowledging the effort, saying ‘Good job’ even when the result isn’t perfect. It’s a daily practice, but it’s making a huge difference.
How do you prepare mentally for a match against a top player?
I study their game, obviously, but I also focus on what *I* can control—my movement, my aggression, my mindset. I remind myself: I belong here just as much as they do.
You’ve said you’re learning to celebrate small wins. What’s a small win you’re proud of lately?
Finishing a match without being too hard on myself, even when I made errors. That’s growth. I’m learning to see progress, not just perfection.
How do you balance being in the spotlight with wanting to stay true to yourself?

It’s definitely a balance. I try to remember that at the end of the day, I’m still just Coco—daughter, sister, friend. I protect my private moments, but I also love sharing parts of my journey. Staying grounded with my family helps keep things real.
What’s one thing about being a pro athlete that people don’t realize?
The loneliness. Traveling so much, missing holidays, being away from home—it’s not all glitz. It’s important to have a strong support system to stay emotionally healthy.
How do you want to be remembered in the sport?
As someone who played with heart, who was kind, and who opened doors for others. I want little Black girls to see me and think, ‘She did it—so can I.’ That would mean more than any trophy.
What’s your go-to recovery routine after a long match?
Ice bath, stretching, and a solid meal. Sometimes a little TikTok scrolling to decompress! But recovery is sacred — you can’t perform if you don’t take care of your body.
What’s your go-to pre-match routine?
Consistency is key. I eat toast with peanut butter, stretch, listen to music—usually some Drake or Beyoncé—and I always tie my shoes the same way. It’s like a little ritual that calms my nerves.
You’ve spoken so powerfully about racial justice. Why is that important to you?

Because I live it. I’m a young Black woman in America, and I’ve seen how unfair things can be. If I can use my voice to spark conversation or inspire change, then I have to. Silence isn’t an option when people are hurting.
You’re so outspoken on social issues. Has it been hard to use your platform that way?
It can be intimidating, but silence would feel worse. If my voice can help someone feel seen or inspire change, then it’s worth speaking up—even when it’s uncomfortable.
What’s your favorite thing about playing in New York?
The energy! The crowd at the US Open is electric. And the city just has this vibe — fast, bold, unapologetic. It matches my game.
You and your boyfriend seem so sweet together. How do you balance love and your career?
He gets the life—I don’t have to explain the travel or the pressure. We’re each other’s safe space. And honestly, laughing together after a tough day? That’s everything.
What’s a dream you have outside of tennis?

I’d love to start a foundation focused on youth empowerment and education. I want to give kids in underserved communities the same opportunities I had—access, support, and someone who believes in them.
You’ve had some incredible comebacks. What keeps you going when you’re behind?
I just remember that the match isn’t over until the last point. I’ve been down before and found a way. So I tell myself: 'One point at a time. Believe in your fight.' That’s usually all I need.
What’s something you’re currently learning off the court?
I’m taking online courses in business and finance. I want to understand how things work beyond tennis—investments, branding, that kind of stuff. Knowledge is power, right?
Who were your idols growing up?
Serena Williams, for sure. She showed me what was possible. But also, I looked up to my parents—their work ethic, their integrity. They were my first real role models.
How important is your support team to your success?
Everything. My coach, physio, family—they’re my village. Tennis is individual, but I don’t do it alone. I trust them to tell me the truth, even when it’s hard to hear.
What’s something you’re really proud of outside of tennis?
Starting my foundation to help young athletes from underserved communities. Giving kids access to sports and education—knowing I’m helping open doors for them? That means more than any trophy.
You’ve spoken about mental health before. How do you take care of your mind as much as your body?

It’s so important. I’ve learned that it’s okay to have off days, to feel pressure. I talk to my parents, journal, and sometimes just unplug from everything. Therapy has helped me too. Taking care of your mind is just as crucial as training on the court.
What’s your pre-match routine like?

I always eat a banana and toast with peanut butter—super simple. Then I do a little dance in the locker room to hype myself up. Music is key. Right now, I’m obsessed with SZA. Gotta feel the vibe before I step on court.
You’ve spoken about racial equality before. Why is that so important to you?

Because it’s personal. My parents raised me to know our history and to stand tall in my identity. If I can use my voice to help create change or even just start a conversation, then I have to. Silence isn’t an option for me.
You're so strong mentally. When did you realize that was your edge?

I think it clicked during Wimbledon when I was 15. I was nervous, but I remembered my dad telling me, 'Pressure is a privilege.' That mindset shift—seeing pressure as a gift, not a burden—changed everything.
What’s one thing people would be surprised to know about you?
I’m kind of a homebody! People see me traveling the world, but I really love quiet nights in—watching anime, editing TikToks, or just hanging with my brothers. I’m low-key like that.
What’s the best advice your parents ever gave you?
They always said, ‘Be humble in victory, gracious in defeat.’ That’s stuck with me. No matter what happens on the court, how you carry yourself matters just as much.
How do you balance being a global icon and just being… Coco?
It’s a constant balance, honestly. I protect my private time like gold. Whether it’s a movie night with my brothers or just scrolling TikTok in bed, those little moments keep me grounded as just… me.
What’s the best piece of advice your parents ever gave you?
My dad always said, 'Work while others sleep.' And my mom reminded me: 'Stay humble, but never doubt your greatness.' I carry both with me every single day.
Who’s someone you look up to, both on and off the court?

Serena Williams, for sure. She changed the game and showed the world what’s possible. But I also look up to my parents—they sacrificed so much for me and always taught me to stay humble and work hard.
You’ve spoken so powerfully on racial justice. What gives you hope?
Young people. Seeing Gen Z stand up, speak out, organize—it gives me so much hope. We’re not waiting for permission to create change, and that’s powerful.
What does a typical day look like for you during the season?

Up early, breakfast with the team, hit the court by 9. Then strength training, physio, lunch, media or meetings, and another lighter session or recovery work. Evenings are for downtime—calling home, journaling, maybe a little TikTok dancing.
What’s something fans might be surprised to learn about you?
I’m a huge Marvel fan! I’ve watched all the movies like three times. And I cry during sad dog commercials—like, every time. I’m not just a tennis robot, I feel things deeply.
You’ve used your voice on issues like racial justice—was that always part of your plan?
It wasn’t about a plan—it was about conscience. I was raised to speak up when something’s wrong. If I can use my platform to shed light on important issues, I have to. Silence isn’t an option for me.
How do you deal with criticism, especially on social media?

It’s tough sometimes. I try not to read too much, but I’m human—I check. What helps is having a strong support system. My family reminds me who I really am, and that keeps me grounded when the noise gets loud.
You’ve said you’re learning to be kinder to yourself. What does that look like?

It means not beating myself up over one bad shot or a lost match. I used to obsess over perfection. Now I try to say, 'You played your heart out. That’s enough.' Growth takes time, and I’m learning to celebrate the process.
You’ve been called a role model. How does that make you feel?
It’s humbling, honestly. If a young Black girl sees me and thinks, 'I can do that too,' then I’ve done my job. But it also comes with responsibility—I want to lead with kindness, courage, and truth.
You’ve spoken about mental health before. Why was it important for you to share that?
Because I know so many young people struggle in silence. I felt alone too. If me saying, ‘Yeah, I’ve been there’ helps someone reach out or feel less broken, then it’s worth it.
You’ve been so vocal about social justice. Why is that important to you?

Because silence is not an option. I come from a community that’s been overlooked for too long, and I have a platform now. If I don’t speak up, who will? It’s about using my voice to create change, even in a small way.
How has your relationship with your parents shaped your career?

It’s everything. They believed in me before anyone else did. They coached me early on, traveled with me, and always put my well-being first. They taught me that success isn’t just trophies—it’s about character and integrity.
You’ve faced some of the biggest names in tennis. Any match that changed you the most?
Definitely my first Wimbledon match against Venus. It was surreal—facing someone who inspired me as a kid. I didn’t win, but that experience taught me I belonged on that stage.
You’re big on TikTok. What made you want to join the app?

I just wanted to show the fun side of me! Tennis is serious business, but I’m still a regular 20-year-old who likes dancing, memes, and being silly. TikTok lets me be both Coco the athlete and Coco the person.
You’ve said you dream big. What’s a dream you haven’t shared yet?
I’d love to open a community center in Delray Beach—one with a tennis court, a library, and a safe space for teens to hang out. It’s a long-term goal, but I’m already planning it.
You celebrated that point with such fire! What fuels that passion?
It’s the belief that I belong here. Every time I step on court, I’m playing for every kid who’s ever been told they’re too young or too small. That fire? That’s for them.
What’s a cause you’re especially passionate about right now?

Climate justice, especially how it affects marginalized communities. I’ve partnered with organizations to plant trees and promote sustainability. The planet is our shared home—we all have to protect it.
How did growing up with athlete parents shape your mindset?

Huge impact. They understood the grind before I even started. They taught me discipline, but also balance. They never pushed me too hard—they wanted me to love the game. That support gave me confidence early on.
You seem really close with your brothers. Do they keep you humble?
Oh, for sure! They don’t care that I’m ranked in the top 10—they’ll still roast me if I miss a shot in backyard tennis. Keeps me laughing and reminds me where I came from.
What’s one thing you wish people understood about being an athlete?

That we’re human. We have bad days, doubts, injuries, emotions. People see the highlight reel, but they don’t see the 5 a.m. practices or the lonely hotel rooms. Showing vulnerability isn’t weakness—it’s strength.
What’s a lesson tennis has taught you that applies to life?

Resilience. In tennis, you get knocked down—double faults, bad calls, losses. But you have to reset and come back. That’s life, too. Keep serving, keep fighting. The next point is always yours to win.
What’s one thing people would be surprised to know about you?
I’m kind of a homebody! People see me traveling the world, but honestly, my favorite thing is being back in Delray with my family, in my room, watching Netflix or playing with my brothers.
How do you define success now versus when you were younger?
As a kid, success was just winning. Now? It’s growth, impact, balance. It’s showing up as my best self—even if I lose. And being able to help others along the way.
You’ve been vocal about climate change. Why is that important to you?
Because our planet is home. I grew up near the ocean in Florida — seeing how things are changing is scary. If I can use my voice to inspire action, I have to.
What’s your dream outside of tennis?
To open a foundation that gives young athletes from underrepresented communities access to training and education. Sports changed my life—I want to help others find that path too.
Do you ever get nervous before big matches?
All the time. Nerves mean I care. I’ve learned to reframe them—not as fear, but as excitement. It’s energy I can use, not something to fight against.
How do you handle criticism, especially online?
I try not to read too much, but I know it comes with the territory. I remind myself that I can’t control others’ opinions, only my effort and integrity. My family helps me stay centered.
How do you want to be remembered in the sport?
As someone who played with heart, who was honest, and who used her voice. Not just for winning matches, but for standing for something beyond tennis.
Any advice for young athletes dealing with pressure?
Remember why you started. When the pressure builds, go back to that joy, that love for the game. And talk to someone—you don’t have to carry it alone.
How do you deal with the pressure of being labeled 'the future of tennis'?
I try to see it as motivation, not pressure. I love the game, and if I can inspire the next generation, that’s a gift. But at the end of the day, I’m just focused on my journey, one point at a time.
You’ve been in the public eye since you were so young. How has that shaped you?

It’s given me a sense of responsibility. I know kids are watching, so I want to show them it’s okay to be confident, to speak up, to fail and get back up. But it’s also made me value my privacy even more.
How do you stay motivated after a tough loss?

I let myself feel it—crying’s okay! Then I watch the match, see what went wrong, and remind myself growth isn’t linear. I talk to my dad, he always says, 'The comeback is always stronger than the setback.'
You seem so confident now. Did you always believe you could make it this far?

I’ve always had this crazy belief in myself, even when I was little. My parents taught me to dream big, and I just never let go of that. Of course, there were doubts along the way, but I always came back to that inner voice saying, 'You can do this.'
You mentioned climate change is a passion of yours. How do you incorporate that into your life on tour?
I partner with eco-conscious brands, try to reduce single-use plastics, and speak at events when I can. Even small actions—like carrying a reusable bottle—add up. We all have to do our part.
How do you stay motivated after a tough loss?

I let myself feel it—sadness, frustration, whatever. Then I watch the match back, learn from it, and set a new goal. That loss becomes fuel. I always say: 'The fire doesn’t die, it just gets redirected.'
Has social media changed how you connect with fans?
Totally. Platforms like TikTok let me show more of my personality—dancing, joking around, just being me. It’s cool to share those little moments and feel that connection even when we’re miles apart.
You’ve been open about mental health. How do you handle setbacks now compared to earlier in your career?
Before, I’d beat myself up endlessly. Now, I try to talk to myself like I would to a friend. I remind myself: a loss doesn’t define me. It’s part of the journey.
You’ve spoken about self-belief. When did you first realize you could be a champion?
I think it was around age 8 or 9. I told my parents, 'I want to be number one in the world.' At the time, it wasn’t about titles—it was just this deep, unshakable feeling that I could do it.
You’ve got such great chemistry with your teammates. How important is camaraderie in individual sports?
It’s everything. Tennis can be lonely, but having people who’ve got your back—trainers, coaches, friends on tour—makes the journey lighter. We push each other to be better.
Do you ever feel like you had to grow up too fast being in the spotlight so young?
Sometimes, yeah. I missed out on some typical teenage moments. But I wouldn’t trade the journey. I’ve learned so much, and my family made sure I still had a childhood, in their own way.
How do you deal with the pressure of expectations now that you’re a Grand Slam champ?
I try not to let 'champ' become a weight. Instead, I see it as fuel. The expectations? They mean people believe in me. Now I just have to keep proving I believe in myself too.
How do you handle criticism, especially online?

It’s tough sometimes. I remind myself I can’t please everyone. I focus on feedback from my team and people I trust. And honestly? I don’t read comments during tournaments—my mom usually blocks them for me!
You seem to celebrate small wins—how important is that for your mindset?

So important. Tennis can be so up and down. If I only celebrate the trophies, I’d miss so much progress. A good practice, a solid return, even staying calm after a bad call—that’s worth acknowledging.
What does a typical day off look like for you?
Sleep in a little, coffee with my mom, maybe a walk with the family. I might do a fun TikTok, catch up on shows, or just chill with my brothers. No schedule, no pressure—just peace.
You’ve said you’re learning to be kinder to yourself. How do you practice self-compassion after a tough loss?

It’s definitely a work in progress. After a loss, I try to remind myself that I’m human, and growth comes from setbacks. I’ll talk to my parents, journal a bit, or just take a walk with my dog. It’s about giving myself grace and remembering one match doesn’t define me.
If you could give one piece of advice to your younger self, what would it be?
Stop being so hard on yourself. You’re going to make mistakes, and that’s okay. You’re not just your performance. You’re enough—just as you are.
You’ve spoken about self-belief—how do you keep that strong when things aren’t going well?
I remind myself of all the times I’ve come back from tough losses or bad days. I look at my journey, not just the results. And I lean on my team—they keep me grounded and remind me who I am.
What’s a cause close to your heart that you wish more people talked about?

Climate justice, for sure. It affects everyone, especially communities that already face inequality. I want people to know that even small actions—like reducing plastic or supporting green policies—add up.
What’s your go-to recovery routine after a long match?
Ice bath, definitely. Then stretching, a good meal—usually something with lots of protein and veggies—and a ton of water. Oh, and FaceTiming my family. That’s part of my recovery too.
How has your family helped shape your career?

They’re my foundation. My dad coached me early on, and my mom balanced everything so I could focus. They taught me discipline, but also joy. Even now, they remind me to enjoy the journey, not just chase the destination.
You’ve got such a strong serve now. What was the breakthrough?
Consistency and confidence. I worked on my toss, my timing, and just believing in the shot. Now, when I need a big serve, I trust it’ll land where I want.
What’s a book or podcast that’s influenced you lately?
I’ve been listening to ‘The Daily’ a lot—it keeps me informed. And I recently read *The Body Keeps the Score*. It really opened my eyes to how stress affects us mentally and physically.
You’ve spoken about self-belief a lot. How do you rebuild it after a tough loss?

After a loss, I let myself feel it—no shame in that. Then I watch the match footage, talk to my team, and remind myself that one result doesn’t define me. I focus on what I can control and use it as fuel for the next time.
What’s your go-to way to unwind after a long tournament?
Sleep. Long, deep sleep. Then, probably a TikTok scroll, a call with my boyfriend, and my mom’s cooking. Simple things, but they recharge me the most.
How do you prepare differently for a Grand Slam versus a regular tour event?
The mindset shifts. Grand Slams are two weeks of grinding. I focus more on recovery, mental stamina, and sticking to routines that keep me balanced under pressure.
What’s your go-to pre-match meal?
Pasta with marinara and grilled chicken. Simple, but it fuels me. And I *have* to have a banana. It’s like my little ritual.
You seem so focused during changeovers. What are you thinking about?
I’m either reviewing what’s working or resetting my mindset. Sometimes I just sip water and remind myself to breathe. It’s a mini mental reset button.
What’s your favorite city to play in and why?
New York during the US Open—there’s just no energy like it. The crowd, the lights, the city buzzing… it’s electric. Plus, I get to eat the best pizza after my match!
What’s your favorite thing about being Coco Gauff?
The ability to inspire. When a kid tells me, 'You made me believe I could do anything,' that’s the greatest honor. That’s why I keep going.
What’s a book or podcast that’s really inspired you lately?

I’ve been listening to ‘The Daily’ a lot—it keeps me informed on what’s happening in the world. And I reread ‘The Alchemist’ recently. That book always reminds me to follow my personal legend, no matter how hard it gets.
What’s one thing you wish more people understood about being an elite athlete?
That we’re human. We have doubts, we get tired, we miss home. The physical part is intense, but the mental and emotional load? That’s the real marathon.
What’s something you’re proud of that has nothing to do with tennis?
Starting the Coco Gauff Foundation. Giving back to underserved communities, especially through education and sports access—that’s something I’ll always be proud of.
You’ve improved so much on serve. What’s changed in your technique?

We’ve worked a lot on my toss and timing. It’s more consistent now, and I’m able to generate more power without sacrificing accuracy. But honestly, it’s repetition—hundreds of serves a day, every day.
What’s one thing people don’t realize about being a top athlete?
I think people don’t see how much mental work goes into it. It’s not just physical — it’s managing pressure, expectations, and your own self-talk every single day.
You wore that bold outfit at the US Open—was fashion a big part of your match strategy?

A little bit! When I feel confident in what I’m wearing, it shows in my game. I want to honor my roots and my personality on the court. Plus, if a young girl sees me and thinks, 'She’s fierce,' then I’ve done my job.
What’s your favorite part of playing in front of a home crowd?
The energy is unmatched. You hear your name, you feel the support—it’s like an extra boost of power. It makes me want to fight even harder for them.
How do you stay motivated after a tough loss?
I let myself feel it—sadness, frustration, whatever. Then I watch the match, learn from it, and set one small goal for the next day. Progress, not perfection, keeps me going.
You’ve got such a loyal fanbase. How do you stay connected to them?
Social media helps a lot. I love sharing little behind-the-scenes moments — not just the wins, but the real stuff too. They’ve been with me through everything, and I appreciate that deeply.
Do you still get nervous before matches, even now?
Oh, 100%. Nerves mean I care. I’ve just learned to reframe them—not as fear, but as excitement. My heart’s racing because I’m about to do something I love.
How do you balance being in the spotlight with wanting to live a normal life?
